fixes.explanation: That's what she says: "Blessed be my son by the LORD!" (Judges 17:2) Picture it. Her silver is gone, Micah says he heard her utter a curse about it, and then her own boy says he took it. I would have expected a very different speech, friend.
That's a natural guess, friend. But she doesn't say shame. She says, "Blessed be my son by the LORD!" (Judges 17:2) Her words aren't what I'd have seen coming at all.

That's a fair guess, since Micah had heard her utter a curse about the silver. But what she says is, "Blessed be my son by the LORD!" (Judges 17:2) She goes from a curse to a blessing. That's a faster turnaround than my oven preheating.
That one belongs to a different story. The text says nothing about a lampstand or the tabernacle here. She says she'll use the silver "…to make a graven image and a molten idol." (Judges 17:3)

Yes, the graven image and molten idol "…were placed in the house of Micah." (Judges 17:4) Two hundred shekels of silver went to a silversmith, and the finished pieces ended up under Micah's roof. That's quite a trip for some silver, friend.
Not a field. The verse says they "…were placed in the house of Micah." (Judges 17:4) These weren't set out under the sky. They were put indoors.

That's right, Micah "…ordained one of his sons as his priest." (Judges 17:5) He keeps the priest job inside his own family. The verse says he had a shrine and made an ephod and some household idols, and then he picked a son for the job.
No brothers in this verse, friend. Micah "…ordained one of his sons as his priest." (Judges 17:5) When Micah needed a priest, he looked to his own boys. Not a single brother got called up.

That's right. The young Levite "…left the city of Bethlehem in Judah to settle where he could find a place." (Judges 17:8) The text gives his own reason for leaving, and it isn't a message from Micah. He came to Micah's house as he traveled.

That's the offer: "…ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions." (Judges 17:10) Micah asks him to "…be my father and priest…" Ten silver shekels, a suit and his provisions, and the young man goes in and agrees to stay.
Close, but the text says "…the young man became like a son to Micah." (Judges 17:11) Look at the flip, friend. Micah asked him to be his father, and he became like a son. A brother doesn't come up.
